title: Nala's bridge
hookLine: five days, a whole army of builders, and the later stories that teach the power of Rama's name
carry: nama: Rama's name carries the stones

cards: Nala steps forward, and what he says is quietly funny. The ocean is right. I'm Vishvakarma's son, and I have my father's skill.

I can build this. Then he adds, more or less: nobody asked me, so I didn't mention it. An army has been staring at an impossible sea, and the one person who could solve it was standing in the crowd, waiting to be asked.

teach.b: Valmiki loves the noise of it. The monkeys and bears pour into the forests and tear up trees by the thousand. They drag boulders down from the hills and heave them into the water with a sound like thunder.
Some hold measuring lines while others lay the stones. And he counts the days: fourteen yojanas the first day, twenty the second, then twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three.

In five days it's done, a hundred yojanas long, straight across the sea, and the army crosses to the shore of Lanka. Two beloved stories aren't in Valmiki. They come from later retellings and oral tradition.
In one, a little squirrel rolls in the sand and shakes it onto the bridge, and Rama strokes its back; the stripes are his fingers. No offering is too small.
In the other, Rama's name is written on the stones, and the stones float.
That one carries a teaching Hindus take very seriously: nama, the divine name. In bhakti, God's name isn't just a label. Saying it, singing it, even writing it, is a way of being with God.
The poet-saint Tulsidas goes further: he calls Rama's name greater than Rama himself, and many devotees read the floating stones that way: the name carries what hands can't.
That's why many devotees fill whole notebooks with Sri Rama, written over and over, as a quiet prayer.

how: Many devotees practice likhita japa, writing Rama's name over and over in notebooks; pilgrims visit Rameswaram and Dhanushkodi, linked by tradition to the bridge, and the squirrel's story is a common children's tale.

games.why: the floating stones come from later retellings, and Hindus tell them for the teaching of nama: the name of God carries what hands can't.

practice: Many devotees practice likhita japa, written repetition: they write a name of God, Sri Rama, again and again, slowly, in a notebook kept just for that. Try a few lines now, on paper or in your mind.
If you pray, write Rama, or the name of God that's yours, and let each one be a small stone on the bridge. If you don't, write one word that steadies you, slowly, and breathe between them.

wordCard.voice: The bridge. Setu. Built in five days by an army of monkeys and bears under Nala, a hundred yojanas long, carried by the ocean that promised to hold it up.

orig.note: Sanskrit setubandha: the binding, or building, of the bridge; also the name given to the place.

carryVoice: Your line: nama, Rama's name carries the stones. Tomorrow, a step back in time, into Ravana's hall. That's day six hundred thirty-six.
